catalog_quote: C'est une langue douce, agréable, quoique d'une prononciation difficile à saisir. Il y a surtout une lettre fort difficile à prononcer; c'est le L qui tient en même temps du R et du D. (La langue Batetela plus dure, gutturale, emploie franchement le R.) Dans un mot de deux syllabes, l'accent tonique est sur la première; dans un mot de trois ou quatre syllabes, il tombe sur l'avant-dernière. Très rares exceptions. Le Musongo chante sa phrase. A la fin de chaque proposition, il ajoute un ô prolongé.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Het Kisongye toonsysteem verschilt radicaal van dat van het Tshiluba. Het Tshiluba bezit een « onverschoven of stationnair » syllabisch toonsysteem dat men comparatief beschouwd inversief of omgekeerd mag heten. [...] Het Kisongye is wel een syllabische, doch verschoven toontaal. Het is in grondbeginsel een verschuiving van het etymologische type, één klankgreep naar rechts. Dit wil zeggen dat men de toon, veroorzaakt door klankgreep a, op b enz. moet zoeken. In de verbale vormen van het werkwoord is het systeem zuiver bewaard, doch drie toonwetten toepasselijk op de laatste klankgreep van de naamwoorden maken de toon van het klinkersuffix doorgaans onbepaalbaar.
new_statements.translation: The Kisongye tone system differs radically from that of Tshiluba. Tshiluba has an 'unshifted or stationary' syllabic tone system which, viewed comparatively, may be called inverted. [...] Kisongye is a syllabic but shifted tone language. In principle it is a shift of the etymological type by one syllable to the right, i.e. the tone caused by syllable a is to be looked for on b, etc. In the verbal forms the system is preserved intact, but three tone rules applying to the last syllable of nouns generally make the tone of the vowel suffix indeterminable. (Supporting first-hand statement, Lumeka 1967, Africana Linguistica 3, p. 41, French: 'Le système tonologique du songye est celui des langues à tons déplacés, c'est-à-dire « chaque mot séparé a ses tons, mais s'il est combiné avec d'autres mots, les tons se déplacent d'une ou de deux syllabes ». Dans notre graphie, toute syllabe dépourvue de signe de tonalité (accent) a le tonème bas.' = 'The tonological system of Songye is that of the languages with shifted tones, i.e. each word in isolation has its tones, but combined with other words the tones shift by one or two syllables. In our spelling every syllable without a tone mark (accent) has low toneme.')

The companion (lines 88-100) has scanned slips (…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Songye is a lexical-tone language (H/L syllabic tones, historically shifted one syllable rightward relative to the etymological pattern, with tone shift across word boundaries in phrases and verb-final metatony ku-sep-a vs ku-sep-á mfumu per Stappers 1964 as reported by Hyman 2017). No opened source makes any statement about word stress; Lumeka's 'accent' refers only to the tone diacritic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; for tone, Stappers notes three tone rules on the final syllable of nouns that neutralise the tone of the vowel suffix, and Lumeka notes tones shift by one or two syllables in combination.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements are about lexical/word tone and its phrasal shifting; no citation-form vs phrase stress distinction is drawn because stress is never discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statements concern Kisongye proper (Stappers 1953, data from his Kasayi mission stations; Lumeka 1967, a native-speaker linguist writing on 'la langue songye' without naming a dialect). Stappers' 1952 tone study and 1964 morphology are of Southern Songye (Bwina Milembwe). Stappers 1962 (examined, not quoted) is of Musolo, an Ilande/Bwilande dialect that Stappers places between Songye and Luba-Katanga and declines to count as Songye outright, although Glottolog files Kilande under song1303 (Mpoyi 1979).

new_statements.quote: Une particularité du Kisonge, c’est que certains mots ont l’accent sur la dernière syllabe, p. ex. Ben ’Ekī, Balā, Lutobō.
new_statements.translation: A peculiarity of Kisonge is that certain words have the accent on the last syllable, e.g. Ben 'Ekī, Balā, Lutobō.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Van Overbergh 1908 p. 347: disyllables initial, tri-/quadrisyllables penultimate, 'Très rares exceptions'): Samain does not restate the default but names a small lexical class of words with FINAL accent, i.e. he identifies what Van Overbergh's 'rare exceptions' look like (note Balā is a disyllable with final accent, against Van Overbergh's initial accent for disyllables, but Samain flags it as exceptional). It neither confirms nor denies penultimate default placement, and it does not address Stappers 1953's statement that Kisongye is a (shifted) syllabic tone language; Samain's macrons could equally reflect final vowel length or high tone heard as accent.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Samain gives no general rule for where the accent falls; his only accent statement is that, as a peculiarity of Kisonge, certain words (his examples are the ethnonyms Ben 'Eki and Bala and the name Lutobo, printed with a macron on the final vowel) carry the accent on the LAST syllable. The default (non-final) position is implied but not stated. The Grammaire (pp. 11-34) opens directly with the noun classes and has no phonetics or accent chapter; the only other prosody-adjacent remark is p. 18 (view f020): 'Quand on veut désigner un objet très éloigné, on appuie sur la dernière lettre de la forme éloignée. Ex. : muntuwa.' (emphatic lengthening/stress of the final segment of distal demonstratives), which is expressive, not word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: The statement itself is a list of exceptions: 'certains mots' with final accent, examples Ben 'Ekī, Balā, Lutobō (macrons in the print may mark the accented/long final vowel).
new_statements.identity_note: Samain describes 'le Kisonge universel' as spoken at Kabinda (Lomami, Kasai, Belgian Congo), the koine of the Basonge sub-tribes (Bekalebwe, Ben' Eki, Bala, Basongo, Bena Kibeshi, Bena Milembwe, etc.), i.e. Songe/Kisongye L23 = song1303; he notes each sub-tribe has some words of its own. Van Overbergh 1908 (catalog source) compiles reports on the Basonge of the same region; Stappers 1953 treats Kisongye in general (his 1952 paper treats the southern Bwina Milembwe variety).

new_statements.quote: Le Kisonge a sa physionomie propre, vu qu’il a un bon nombre de mots qu’on ne trouve ni dans le Kiluba-Hemba ni dans le Tshiluba du Kasai. On est amené à penser que les Basonge ont été en contact avec d’autres tribus. Une particularité du Kisonge, c’est que certains mots ont l’accent sur la dernière syllabe, p. ex. Ben ’Ekī, Balā, Lutobō. Le Kisonge n’est pas facile; un Muluba du Kasai doit l’apprendre pendant quelques semaines avant de le connaître.
new_statements.translation: Kisonge has its own character, since it has a good number of words found neither in Kiluba-Hemba nor in the Tshiluba of Kasai. One is led to think that the Basonge have been in contact with other tribes. A peculiarity of Kisonge is that certain words have the accent on the last syllable, e.g. Ben 'Ekī, Balā, Lutobō. Kisonge is not easy; a Muluba of Kasai has to study it for some weeks before knowing it.

tone_statements.quote: 1.2.4. Système tonale Le Kisongye (kikaleebwe) atteste deux tons simples ; haut (∕) et bas (\) ainsi que deux tons complexes : montant (v) et descendant (^). Voici les exemples en rapport avec différents tons : Tons simples Tons complexes Kulootá= rêver haut Mbǒ = le buffle montant Milòmò= les lèvres bas Mwâna= un enfant descendant Il est à démontrer que le ton montant(v) et le ton descendant (^) résultent de la fusion du ton haut(∕) et du ton bas ou (\).
tone_statements.translation: 1.2.4. Tone system. Kisongye (Kikaleebwe) attests two simple tones: high and low, as well as two complex tones: rising and falling. Here are examples for the different tones: simple tones / complex tones: kulootá 'to dream' high; mbǒ 'the buffalo' rising; milòmò 'the lips' low; mwâna 'a child' falling. It is to be shown that the rising tone and the falling tone result from the fusion of the high tone and the low tone.
tone_statements.summary: 2 level tones H, L plus rising and falling contours (= H+L combinations); Kalebwe (northern) Songye.

tone_statements.citation: Schadeberg, Thilo C. 1995. Object diagnostics in Bantu. In E. 'Nolue Emenanjo & Ozo-mekuri Ndimele (eds.), Issues in African Languages and Linguistics: Essays in Honour of Kay Williamson (Special issue of Nigerian Language Studies), 173-180. Aba: National Institute for Nigerian Languages. Open access: hdl:1887/8832 (Leiden Scholarly Publications; PDFhttps://scholarlypublications.universiteitleiden.nl/access/item%3A2883325/download).
tone_statements.quote: I shall use Stappers’ (1964) grammar of Songye (L.23) for exemplification. From the description it is clear that the high tone final °-á appears before an object and the low tone final °-a before pause. Note that it is quite clear that this is not a phonological conditioning since numerous other words, including verb forms, are consistently ending in either high or low tones irrespective of their being in the middle or at the end of a phrase. … (5) Songye L.23 (Stappers 1964) kudimununa to work again (on the land) kudimununá mádimi to work the fields again kusepá mfumu to laugh at the chief
tone_statements.summary: Comparative Bantu syntax paper: in Songye the infinitive’s final suffix is high before an object, low otherwise (metatony); other words end in fixed high or low tones. No tone inventory stated.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction. The catalog rule (Van Overbergh 1908 p. 347: initial accent in disyllables, penultimate in tri- and quadrisyllables, 'très rares exceptions') is not restated by Samain [1924], whose only accent sentence (Introduction p. 6) says that certain words carry the accent on the LAST syllable (Ben 'Ekī, Balā, Lutobō): this names a lexical class of final-accent exceptions and includes a disyllable (Balā) that Van Overbergh's wording would stress initially, but Samain himself presents these as a peculiarity, so the two are compatible as default-plus-exceptions. The standing tension held by the project is with Stappers 1953 (Aequatoria 16: 3), who describes Kisongye as a syllabic tone language with rightward tone shift and says nothing about stress; neither missionary source (1908, 1924) distinguishes tone or vowel length from 'accent', and Samain's macrons on the final vowels could mark length or high tone rather than stress. No new text was opened, so no new disagreement arises. The standing tension in the record is unchanged: the catalog penultimate stress (penultimate stress) traces to van Overbergh 1908, Les Basonge, p. 347 (an ethnographic compilation), while the only linguist's statement held by the project, Stappers 1953 (Aequatoria 16: 3), describes Kisongye as a syllabic 'shifted' tone language and says nothing about stress. These are not strictly contradictory (penultimate prominence coexisting with lexical/grammatical tone is common in the zone), but…

sources.note: Proverb (paremiology) study whose sec. 1.2 is a short phonological sketch of Kalebwe Songye; sec. 1.2.4 'Système tonale' states two simple tones, high and low, and two complex tones, rising and falling, the contours analysed as fusions of H and L; examples kulootá 'rêver' (H), milòmò 'les lèvres' (L), mbǒ 'le buffle' (rising), mwâna 'un enfant' (falling). No statement on tone-bearing unit, downstep or tone rules; low-authority venue but an explicit first-hand statement for the northern (Kalebwe) variety, consistent with the lexical-tone coding listed here.

tone.translation: 1.2.4. Tone system. Kisongye (Kikaleebwe) attests two simple tones: high and low, as well as two complex tones: rising and falling. Here are examples for the different tones: simple tones / complex tones: kulootá 'to dream' high; mbǒ 'the buffalo' rising; milòmò 'the lips' low; mwâna 'a child' falling. It is to be shown that the rising tone and the falling tone result from the fusion of the high tone and the low tone.
tone.summary: 2 level tones H, L plus rising and falling contours (= H+L combinations); Kalebwe (northern) Songye.
tone.says: Proverb (paremiology) study whose sec. 1.2 is a short phonological sketch of Kalebwe Songye; sec. 1.2.4 'Système tonale' states two simple tones, high and low, and two complex tones, rising and falling, the contours analysed as fusions of H and L; examples kulootá 'rêver' (H), milòmò 'les lèvres' (L), mbǒ 'le buffle' (rising), mwâna 'un enfant' (falling). sources.quote: I shall use Stappers’ (1964) grammar of Songye (L.23) for exemplification. From the description it is clear that the high tone final °-á appears before an object and the low tone final °-a before pause. Note that it is quite clear that this is not a phonological conditioning since numerous other words, including verb forms, are consistently ending in either high or low tones irrespective of their being in the middle or at the end of a phrase. … (5) Songye L.23 (Stappers 1964) kudimununa to work again (on the land) kudimununá mádimi to work the fields again kusepá mfumu to laugh at the chief
sources.note: Comparative Bantu syntax paper: in Songye the infinitive’s final suffix is high before an object, low otherwise (metatony); other words end in fixed high or low tones. No tone inventory stated.

sources.quote: Juist zoals iedere Bantoetaal heeft het Buina Milembwe slechts twee essentiële tonen (grondtonen) : een gelijkmatig hoge en lage toon. [...] Samengestelde tonen, zoals stijgend en dalend, komen enkel voor in twee tijden tellende klankgrepen. Het is derhalve de resultante van laag + hoog, resp. hoog + laag. Een gelijkmatige middelhoge toon komt als grondtoon niet voor. [...] In de woordleer heeft de toonhoogte een semantische en in de spraakkunst een grammaticale functie. [...] dan stellen we vooreerst vast dat het syllabisch is; d. w. z. dat er aan elke klankgreep een hoge of lage toon verbonden is. || De toon verbonden aan een bepaalde klankgreep, komt te rusten op de onmiddellijk volgende klankgreep ; m. a. w. de klankgreep die een bepaalde toon eist of veroorzaakt, en de klankgreep welke deze toon draagt, zijn niet identiek. Een dergelijk toonsysteem noemen we verschoven.
sources.locator: pp. 200-201, section A.I 'Type van toonsysteem : verschoven syllabisch'; tone laws pp. 207-209 (PDF 9-11); noun tone groups and minimal pairs pp. 217-221 (PDF…
sources.note: Confirms the catalog tone class (lexical-tone): two level tones H and L, no mid tone; rising and falling only on two-mora syllables as L+H / H+L; every syllable carries H or L (syllabic); tone has a semantic (lexical) function in the lexicon and a grammatical function in the grammar. The system is of the 'verschoven' (shifted) type: the tone a syllable demands is realised on the immediately following syllable, across word boundaries from the first syllable of a sentence to the last (pp. 200-201). Sentence-initial syllable assimilates to the second (p. 202); an isolated word gets H on its first
